kurz.s: How independent is the dealership of banks and the manufacturer?
g: the owners' money, stays in the business permanently
share of equity in total capital
how much debt there is per 1 € of equity
kurz.b: Balance sheet total 4,0 m €, equity 0,6 m €, debt 3,4 m €, mainly purchase financing for the vehicles.
kurz.c:
Equity ratio    0,6 / 4,0 × 100 =  15 %
Debt-to-equity  3,4 / 0,6 × 100 = 567 %
kurz.f: Assess the equity ratio of 15 % and name one consequence for the loan meeting.
kurz.x: Because their vehicle stock is financed, dealerships often have low equity ratios. Always assess with a comparison (previous year, industry), not just „high“ or „low“.
a: 15 % is low: only a small part of the capital belongs to the owners, the dealership depends heavily on the bank and the manufacturer.
Consequence: the bank rates creditworthiness lower and asks for higher interest or more security.
kurz.m: Equity ratio = equity / total capital × 100 · Debt-to-equity = debt / equity × 100

kurz.t: Fixed asset coverage and the golden balance sheet rule
kurz.s: Are long-term assets financed long term?
g: stay in the business for a long time: buildings, lifts, equipment
finance assets tied up long term with long-term capital
checks exactly this, target: at least 100 %
kurz.b: Fixed assets 1.500 k€, equity 600 k€, long-term loans 750 k€.
kurz.f: Assess fixed asset coverage II and name one measure to improve it.
kurz.x: Below 100 %, part of the fixed assets is financed short term. When the loan runs out, it has to be refinanced, even though the workshop building cannot be sold.
a: 90 % breaks the golden balance sheet rule: 10 % of fixed assets are financed with short-term capital.
Measures: convert short-term loans into long-term loans, increase equity (retain profits, contribution), sell or lease assets that are not needed.
kurz.m: Fixed asset coverage II = (equity + long-term debt) / fixed assets × 100

kurz.s: Can the dealership pay its short-term debts?
g: cash in hand and at the bank only
plus inventories, i.e. all current assets
kurz.b: Bank 60 k€, receivables 140 k€, vehicle stock 900 k€. Short-term liabilities (purchase financing, suppliers) 800 k€.
kurz.f: Assess liquidity level 2 and name two measures to improve it.
kurz.x: At a dealership, the money is tied up in the vehicles. A low level 2 is normal here as long as days in stock are short. Do not automatically write „insolvent“.
a: 25 % is well below the rule of thumb of 100 %. Without selling vehicles, the dealership can only pay a quarter of its short-term debts.
Measures: reduce days in stock, collect receivables faster, convert short-term loans into long-term ones.
kurz.m: Liquidity = respective assets / short-term debt × 100

kurz.s: How well does the money invested pay off?
g: interest earned on the owners' money
interest earned on all capital, interest paid to the bank counts too
how many cents of profit remain from each euro of revenue
kurz.b: Profit 90 k€, interest on debt 60 k€, equity 600 k€, total capital 4.000 k€, revenue 18.000 k€.
kurz.c:
Return on equity  90 / 600 × 100          = 15,00 %
Return on capital (90 + 60) / 4.000 × 100 =  3,75 %
Return on sales   90 / 18.000 × 100       =  0,50 %
kurz.f: Explain why interest on debt is added to profit for the return on total capital.
kurz.x: Do not forget the interest. Profit has already been reduced by the interest, but the borrowed capital earned exactly this interest.
a: Return on total capital measures what all the capital invested has earned.
Profit is the owners' income, interest is the lenders' income. Only both together are the income of the total capital.
kurz.m: ROE = profit / equity × 100 · ROTC = (profit + interest) / total capital × 100 · ROS = profit / revenue × 100

kurz.s: When is more borrowing worthwhile for the owners?
g: debt acts like a lever on the return on equity
return on total capital higher than the loan rate: more debt raises the return on equity
return on total capital lower than the loan rate: debt lowers the return on equity
kurz.b: The dealership earns 8 % on all its capital and pays 5 % interest. Every borrowed euro earns 3 cents more than it costs. This surplus goes to the owners.
kurz.c: Return 8 % − interest 5 % = 3 % advantage per borrowed euro
kurz.f: Assess whether the dealership should finance a new hall with a loan at 9 % when the return on total capital is 6 %.
kurz.x: The lever works both ways. If interest rises above the return, the return on equity falls, and every further loan increases the risk.
a: From a profitability point of view, no: the loan costs 9 %, the capital earns only 6 %.
This is a negative leverage effect: the return on equity falls, dependency and risk increase.
kurz.m: positive leverage effect when return on total capital > interest rate on debt

kurz.s: How much money is in the parts store and for how long?
g: capital tied up in the store
how often the stock is sold and replenished per year
how many days a part stays in stock on average
kurz.b: Parts store: opening stock 110 k€, closing stock 90 k€, cost of goods 800 k€ per year.
kurz.c:
Ø stock          (110 + 90) / 2 = 100 k€
Turnover rate    800 / 100      = 8 times
Storage period   360 / 8        = 45 days
kurz.f: Name two measures to reduce the storage period and one effect of each.
kurz.x: Use the cost of goods at cost price, not revenue at selling prices. Otherwise the turnover rate comes out too high.
a: Sell off slow movers or return them to the manufacturer: less capital tied up, less obsolescence.
Order smaller quantities more often or lower the minimum stock: lower storage interest and storage costs.
Note: too little stock endangers availability for the workshop and customers.
kurz.m: Turnover rate = cost of goods / Ø stock · Storage period = 360 / turnover rate

kurz.s: What did the actual dealership business earn?
g: result of the actual business: output − costs
non-operational, from other periods or extraordinary
both together, as shown in the income statement
kurz.b: The dealership makes an operating profit of 120 k€. A flat rented out above the showroom brings 15 k€, water damage costs 40 k€.
kurz.c:
Operating result   120 k€
Neutral result     15 − 40 = −25 k€
Company result      95 k€
kurz.f: Explain why the operating result says more than the company result when assessing the business units.
kurz.x: Rent from a flat or a gain on shares does not belong to the business. It improves the company result but says nothing about sales and the workshop.
a: The operating result only contains costs and output from the actual purpose: vehicles, parts, workshop.
One-off or non-operational items distort the company result. Without them, the development of the business units can be compared.
kurz.m: Operating result + neutral result = company result

kurz.t: Gross profit and days in stock
kurz.s: What is left over on used cars?
g: revenue minus cost of goods: left for costs and profit
interest, loss of value, space, care, per day
kurz.b: Used cars in the quarter: revenue 400 k€, cost of goods 360 k€. Average 80 days in stock at 14 € holding costs per day.
kurz.c:
Gross profit   40 k€ / 400 k€ × 100 = 10,0 %
Holding costs  80 days × 14 €       = 1.120 € per vehicle
kurz.f: Days in stock rise from 60 to 80. Assess the consequences for gross profit and name two countermeasures.
kurz.x: Long days in stock cost twice: ongoing holding costs and falling prices because the vehicle gets older. Gross profit falls although nothing changed in purchasing.
a: Per vehicle 20 days × 14 € = 280 € more holding costs, plus discounts when selling: gross profit and result fall.
Measures: market-based purchase prices, fast reconditioning, adjust prices regularly, market vehicles over 90 days actively or sell them to dealers.
kurz.m: Gross profit in % = (revenue − cost of goods) / revenue × 100

kurz.s: What belongs in the calculation and what does not?
g: all consumption of value according to the income statement
an expense that is not a cost
kurz.b: Donation to the sports club: neutral (non-operational). Back tax for an earlier year: neutral (other period). Mechanics' wages: basic costs. Imputed entrepreneur's salary: additional costs.
kurz.f: Distinguish between expense and cost and classify a donation to the sports club.
kurz.x: Imputed costs (entrepreneur's salary, interest on equity) are not in the income statement but belong in the calculation. Otherwise prices are too low.
a: An expense is any consumption of value in the period, costs are only the operational, period-related and ordinary part.
The donation is a neutral, non-operational expense and not a cost. It does not belong in the calculation.
kurz.m: Basic costs: expense = cost · Different costs: cost in a different amount · Additional costs: cost without expense

kurz.t: Direct costs, overheads and overhead rate
kurz.s: How do rent and administration get into the price?
g: directly attributable to a job: the part's cost price, productive wages
arise for many jobs: rent, administration, heating
allocates overheads to cost centres and provides the overhead rates
kurz.b: Workshop: overheads 420 k€, productive wages 150 k€.
kurz.c:
Overhead rate  420 / 150 × 100 = 280 %
Job with 200 € wages: 200 + 560 = 760 € total cost
kurz.f: Explain why overheads are charged using an overhead rate.
kurz.x: Watch the base of the cost centre: productive wages in the workshop, cost of goods in vehicle and parts sales.
a: Overheads cannot be assigned directly to a job but must be recovered through prices.
The overhead rate spreads them in proportion to direct costs: whoever causes more direct costs bears more overheads.
kurz.m: Overhead rate = overheads of the cost centre / direct costs × 100

kurz.s: Is an order worthwhile when the fixed costs are there anyway?
g: price minus variable costs: contribution to covering fixed costs
quantity at which all fixed costs are covered
kurz.b: A care kit costs 18 € to buy and sells for 30 € net. The fixed costs of the campaign are 1.800 €.
kurz.c:
CM per unit  30 − 18     = 12 €
Break-even   1.800 / 12  = 150 units
kurz.f: A key customer wants 50 kits at 20 € net. The fixed costs are already covered. Assess the offer.
kurz.x: Do not decide on full costs when the fixed costs arise anyway. In the short term, all that counts is whether the contribution margin is positive.
a: CM per unit 20 − 18 = 2 €, for 50 kits 100 € extra profit.
Accept as long as capacity is sufficient and other customers do not demand the low price as well.
kurz.m: CM per unit = price − variable unit costs · Break-even quantity = fixed costs / CM per unit

kurz.s: From landed cost to list price and back
g: landed cost known, selling price wanted
selling price set by the market, highest purchase price wanted
purchase and selling price fixed, profit wanted
kurz.b: Landed cost 100 €, operating costs 30 %, profit 10 %, customer cash discount 2 %, customer discount 10 %.
kurz.c:
Total cost           100 × 1,3         = 130,00 €
Cash selling price   130 × 1,1         = 143,00 €
Target selling price 143 / 98 × 100    = 145,92 €
List selling price   145,92 / 90 × 100 = 162,13 €
kurz.f: Explain why customer cash discount and customer discount are calculated „im Hundert“.
kurz.x: Do not simply add 2 % and 10 %. The customer deducts discount and cash discount from the higher price, so the price you are looking for is 100 %.
a: Discount and cash discount are deducted from the list or target price, i.e. from the higher value.
The known price is only 90 % or 98 % of it. So you scale up to 100 % (÷ 0,90 or ÷ 0,98).
kurz.m: Target selling price = cash selling price × 100 / (100 − cash discount rate)

kurz.t: Workshop index and hourly labour rate
kurz.s: What must a workshop hour cost?
g: factor used to scale wages up to the selling price
price of a workshop hour for the customer
kurz.b: Average wage 22 €, overhead rate 280 %, profit 10 %, risk 5 %.
kurz.c:
Cost 22 × 3,8 = 83,60 €
+ 10 % profit on 83,60 = 8,36 €
+ 5 % risk on 83,60 = 4,18 €
= target labour revenue = 96,14 €
Index 96,14 / 22 = 4,37
kurz.f: Explain what a workshop index of 4,37 means.
kurz.x: Profit and risk are both calculated on cost, not one after the other. So the percentages can simply be added: 3,8 × 1,15 = 4,37. And: the index is not the overhead rate. 280 % only gives the factor 3,8.
a: For every euro of productive wages, the workshop must earn 4,37 € from the customer.
Only then are wages, all workshop overheads, the risk and the planned profit covered.
kurz.m: Target index = target labour revenue / productive wages · Actual index = actual labour revenue / productive wages · Hourly rate = average wage × index

kurz.s: How many people need to be hired?
g: number of employees needed at the planning date (target)
leavers (retirement, resignation) and joiners (returners, apprentices kept on)
kurz.b: Target 36 positions, actual 35. By the reference date 3 retire, 1 returns from parental leave, 2 apprentices are kept on.
kurz.c:
Projected  35 − 3 + 1 + 2 = 35
Net need   36 − 35        = hire 1 person
kurz.f: Name three foreseeable reasons for filling a position.
kurz.x: Returners from parental leave and apprentices kept on are joiners. Forget them and you hire too many people.
a: Retirement
Maternity protection or parental leave
Resignation with notice, end of a fixed-term contract, promotion or transfer
kurz.m: Net staffing requirement = target − (actual − leavers + joiners)

kurz.s: By when must the notice be received?
g: 4 weeks to the 15th or the end of the month, for both sides
longer periods by length of service, from 2 years 1 month to the end of the month
kurz.b: A mechanic has worked at the dealership for 6 years. The dealership wants to give notice for 30.09.
kurz.c:
from 5 years: 2 months to the end of the month
received by 31.07. at the latest
kurz.f: Determine by when the notice must be received and justify your answer.
kurz.x: What counts is receipt by the employee, not the date sent. The longer periods only apply when the employer gives notice.
a: After 6 years of service, the employer must give 2 months' notice to the end of the month (§ 622 (2) BGB).
For notice to 30.09., it must be received by 31.07. at the latest.
kurz.m: 2 years → 1 month · 5 → 2 · 8 → 3 · 10 → 4 · 12 → 5 · 15 → 6 · 20 → 7 months, each to the end of the month

kurz.s: From gross salary to net pay
g: salary plus e.g. employer VL contribution, basis for social security
SV gross minus tax allowance, basis for tax
8 % (Bavaria, Baden-Württemberg) or 9 % of the wage tax
kurz.b: Salary 3.000 €, 30 years old, childless, wage tax 340 €, church tax 9 %, additional contribution 2,9 %.
kurz.f: Explain why a tax allowance does not reduce social security contributions.
kurz.x: Deduct the allowance for tax only. The employee pays the 0,6 % childless surcharge alone (2,4 % instead of 1,8 %).
a: The allowance is a tax rule and only reduces taxable pay.
Social security is always calculated on the gross subject to social security.
kurz.m: Net = SV gross − wage tax − soli − church tax − health − care − pension − unemployment

kurz.t: The 4 cards and the VAK booking
kurz.s: Why every sale needs two bookings
g: VAK to stock, at cost price
payables to bank or bank to receivables
kurz.b: A set of winter wheels is sold for 600 € net. It was bought for 400 €.
kurz.c:
Receivables 714,00 to revenue 600,00
                     output VAT 114,00
VAK 400,00 to stock 400,00
kurz.f: Make the booking records for the sale and the stock withdrawal.
kurz.x: Every sale needs two bookings: revenue at the selling price and stock withdrawal (VAK) at cost price. The VAK booking is often forgotten in the exam.
a: Receivables 714,00 to revenue 600,00 and output VAT 114,00
VAK 400,00 to stock 400,00
kurz.m: Revenue − VAK = gross profit (here 200 €)

kurz.s: Payment with a deduction, and the tax follows
g: we pay an incoming invoice with a deduction
a customer pays our invoice with a deduction
the discount also reduces input or output VAT
kurz.b: Incoming invoice for parts 1.190 € gross, paid with 2 % cash discount.
kurz.c:
Discount gross 1.190 × 2 % = 23,80
  of which net 20,00, input VAT 3,80
Bank pays                   1.166,20
kurz.f: Make the booking record for the payment with cash discount.
kurz.x: The IHK chart of accounts often has no separate discount account. The net discount then reduces the stock account on purchases and the revenue account on sales. Always correct the tax too.
a: Payables 1.190,00 to bank 1.166,20, stock 20,00 and input VAT 3,80
kurz.m: Net discount = gross discount / 1,19

kurz.s: Used cars bought privately: tax on the margin only
g: bought without input VAT deduction, e.g. from a private person
VAT only on the margin (selling price − purchase price)
no VAT shown, reference to § 25a UStG
kurz.b: Bought privately for 10.000 €, sold for 12.380 €.
kurz.f: Explain why margin taxation exists.
kurz.x: Do not calculate the tax on the whole selling price and do not add 19 % to the margin: the margin is a gross amount, so × 19 / 119.
a: No input VAT could be deducted when buying from a private person.
If the full selling price were taxed, the value of the vehicle would be taxed twice. So only the added value, the margin, is taxed.
kurz.m: VAT = (selling price − purchase price) × 19 / 119

kurz.s: From list purchase price to selling price
g: Deduct the supplier's discount and cash discount, add delivery costs: this gives the landed cost.
Operating costs on the landed cost, profit on the total cost, both calculated „vom Hundert“ (on the known value).
Add customer cash discount and customer discount „im Hundert“ (on the price still to be found), then VAT.
kurz.b: Roof box: list purchase price 400,00 €, supplier discount 20 %, supplier cash discount 2 %, delivery costs 6,40 €, operating costs 25 %, profit 10 %, customer cash discount 2 %, customer discount 5 %.
kurz.c:
List purchase price = 400,00 €
− 20 % supplier discount = 80,00 €
= target purchase price = 320,00 €
− 2 % supplier cash discount = 6,40 €
= cash purchase price = 313,60 €
+ delivery costs = 6,40 €
= landed cost = 320,00 €
+ 25 % operating costs = 80,00 €
= total cost = 400,00 €
+ 10 % profit = 40,00 €
= cash selling price = 440,00 €
+ 2 % customer cash discount (440,00 ÷ 0,98) = 8,98 €
= target selling price = 448,98 €
+ 5 % customer discount (448,98 ÷ 0,95) = 23,63 €
= list selling price net = 472,61 €
+ 19 % VAT = 89,80 €
= gross selling price = 562,41 €
kurz.f: Justify why supplier discount and supplier cash discount are deducted „vom Hundert“, while customer cash discount and customer discount are added „im Hundert“.
kurz.x: Most common mistake: simply adding customer cash discount and customer discount as on the purchasing side. 440,00 × 1,02 = 448,80 € is wrong, correct is 440,00 ÷ 0,98 = 448,98 €. Also: on both sides the cash discount is closer to the cash price than the discount, and delivery costs are only added after the cash discount.
a: On the purchasing side the starting price is the higher value: the supplier grants the discount on the list price and the cash discount on the target price. The known price is 100 %, so you deduct „vom Hundert“.

On the selling side the price you are looking for is the higher one: the customer later deducts cash discount and discount from our target or list price. The known price is only 98 % or 95 % of it, so you calculate „im Hundert“ (÷ 0,98 and ÷ 0,95).
kurz.m: deduct vom Hundert: × (1 − p) · add auf Hundert: × (1 + p) · add im Hundert: ÷ (1 − p)

kurz.s: What is the most the purchase may cost?
g: The selling price is set by the market or by the manufacturer.
the highest list purchase price the dealership may pay
Every step of the forward calculation is reversed: mark-ups become divisions, deductions become additions.
kurz.b: Roof box: market price 535,50 € gross, customer discount 5 %, customer cash discount 2 %, profit 10 %, operating costs 25 %, delivery costs 6,40 €, supplier cash discount 2 %, supplier discount 20 %.
kurz.c:
Gross selling price = 535,50 €
− VAT (÷ 1,19) = 85,50 €
= list selling price net = 450,00 €
− 5 % customer discount (vom Hundert) = 22,50 €
= target selling price = 427,50 €
− 2 % customer cash discount (vom Hundert) = 8,55 €
= cash selling price = 418,95 €
− profit (418,95 ÷ 1,10) = 38,09 €
= total cost = 380,86 €
− operating costs (380,86 ÷ 1,25) = 76,17 €
= landed cost = 304,69 €
− delivery costs = 6,40 €
= cash purchase price = 298,29 €
+ 2 % supplier cash discount (298,29 ÷ 0,98) = 6,09 €
= target purchase price = 304,38 €
+ 20 % supplier discount (304,38 ÷ 0,80) = 76,10 €
= highest list purchase price = 380,48 €
kurz.f: Explain why the profit in the backward calculation must not be deducted as 10 % of the cash selling price.
kurz.x: Do not simply deduct the percentages. 418,95 − 10 % = 377,06 € would be wrong, correct is 418,95 ÷ 1,10 = 380,86 €. Profit and operating costs are divided out, customer discount and customer cash discount are deducted „vom Hundert“, supplier cash discount and supplier discount are added „im Hundert“.
a: In the forward calculation the profit was added as 10 % on the total cost. So the cash selling price equals 110 % of the total cost.

Backwards, the total cost is the base value you are looking for (100 %): cash selling price ÷ 1,10. Deducting 10 % of the cash selling price uses the wrong base value and gives a total cost that is too low.
kurz.m: deduct vom Hundert: × (1 − p) · back auf Hundert: ÷ (1 + p) · add im Hundert: ÷ (1 − p)

ffs.t: Distribution systems in new car retail
ffs.s: The management of Autohaus Nordring GmbH has learned that Nova-Werke AG wants to change its distribution system. You prepare information for the management.

p.q: Autohaus Nordring GmbH is an authorised dealer of Nova-Werke AG. Explain the term 'authorised dealer' (Vertragshändler).
p.a: An authorised dealer is legally independent and bound to the manufacturer by a dealer contract (1 P). It buys the new vehicles and sells them in its own name and for its own account (1 P).

p.q: Explain what direct distribution means and give an example.
p.a: In direct distribution the manufacturer sells to the end customer without an independent dealer (1 P). Examples: manufacturer-owned branch, manufacturer's online direct sales, fleet sales by the manufacturer (1 P).

p.q: Nova-Werke AG plans to switch to a genuine agency system. Explain 2 key features of a genuine agency system from the dealership's point of view.
p.a:
2 points per explained feature, e.g.:
• The dealership sells as an agent in the name and for the account of the manufacturer; the customer's contract partner is the manufacturer.
• The manufacturer sets the selling price; the dealership cannot grant its own discounts.
• The dealership receives an agency commission instead of a margin.
• New vehicles remain the manufacturer's property until sold; the manufacturer bears stock and price risk.

p.q: Name one advantage and one disadvantage of the genuine agency system for the dealership.
p.a: Advantage (1 P), e.g.: less capital tied up, no stock or price risk, no discount negotiations. Disadvantage (1 P), e.g.: no own pricing flexibility, often lower income, greater dependence on the manufacturer, customer data held by the manufacturer.

p.q: State which institution represents the interests of a brand's dealerships towards the manufacturer.
p.a: The dealer association of the brand (2 P); across brands, the central association of the German motor trade (ZDK) represents motor trade businesses.

ffs.s: A customer shows you an offer from an independent dealer for a re-imported Nova Pulse that is much cheaper than your offer. Management is also considering offering pre-registered vehicles at year end.

p.q: Explain what is meant by a re-imported vehicle.
p.a: A vehicle intended for a foreign market (usually another EU country) (1 P), bought there from a dealer (1 P) and brought back to Germany by an independent dealer and sold here (1 P).

p.q: Name 2 reasons why a re-imported vehicle can be cheaper for a German customer.
p.a: 1 point per reason, e.g.: lower net manufacturer prices in countries with high registration taxes; stronger competition abroad; currency advantages; different, often lower equipment.

p.q: The customer asks what claims he has if the re-imported vehicle is defective. Explain the legal position.
p.a: Statutory liability for defects (two years) applies against the seller, i.e. the independent dealer, not against a Nova dealer (1,5 P). The manufacturer's warranty applies EU-wide and can be used at any authorised dealer; however, it may already have started with first delivery abroad and therefore be shorter (1,5 P).

p.q: Explain one possible advantage of a pre-registration for the dealership.
p.a: E.g.: the dealership reaches its sales or registration targets and secures the related bonuses (2 P); alternatively: reducing stock vehicles or selling them at a discount as nearly-new cars.

p.q: Name 2 typical disadvantages of selling pre-registered vehicles.
p.a: 1 point per disadvantage, e.g.: lower revenue due to high discounts; the buyer is the second keeper; warranty and depreciation start at registration; costs of registration and deregistration; disruption of new car pricing.

p.q: Name 2 advantages for Mr Becker if he buys the used car from the dealership rather than privately.

p.q: Mr Becker wants to pay the price of 18.000,00 € in cash. Name the law that applies here and explain the dealership's obligation.
p.a: Money Laundering Act (GwG) (1 P). For cash payments of 10.000,00 € or more, the dealership as a goods dealer must identify the customer, e.g. by copying the ID card (1 P), and record and keep this; suspicious cases must be reported (1 P). Many dealerships therefore refuse large cash payments.

Mr Becker takes out a used car warranty. Distinguish the used car warranty from statutory liability for defects.
p.a: Liability for defects: statutory, covers only defects present at handover (1 P). Warranty: voluntary contractual promise, covers damage to covered parts occurring during its term, often with a customer share (1 P).

p.a: Electronic insurance confirmation (elektronische Versicherungsbestätigung) (1 P). It proves to the registration office that motor liability insurance exists for the vehicle; without it registration is not possible (1 P).

p.q: Before approving the loan, the bank checks legal capacity to borrow and creditworthiness. Explain both terms.
p.a: Capacity to borrow: the legal ability to conclude a loan agreement effectively, i.e. full legal capacity (2 P). Creditworthiness: the personal and economic ability and willingness to repay (credit standing), e.g. income, employment, payment history (2 P).

1 point per correct relationship, e.g.:
• purchase contract between Ms Nguyen and the dealership
• loan agreement between Ms Nguyen and Nova Bank
• the bank pays the loan amount directly to the dealership
• cooperation agreement between dealership and bank (brokering for commission)

p.q: Mr Schröder fears an economic total loss. Explain the term to him.

• It must be paid for and is usually limited to a total mileage.
• Specified components are covered; at higher mileage the customer pays a share of materials.

p.q: Explain the reversal of the burden of proof in consumer sales.
p.a: If a defect appears within one year of handover (1 P), it is presumed to have existed at handover; the seller must prove otherwise (1 P). (§ 477 BGB)

p.q: Another customer has no extended warranty. The manufacturer covers part of the costs as goodwill. Explain the term goodwill and name 2 reasons why manufacturers grant it.
p.a: Goodwill is a voluntary payment without legal obligation, e.g. after the warranty has expired (2 P). Reasons (1 P each), e.g.: customer satisfaction and loyalty, brand image, a known weak point of a component, full service history at an authorised workshop.
